transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-06-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Samira Ortiz (Redwood Product), Priya Nair (ZenLedger SRE), Tom Reynolds (ZenLedger Head of Platform), Luis Gomez (ZenLedger Staff Eng)

Summary:
Quick, hands-on console walkthrough focused on tracing and request-debugging flows. Customer observed intermittent 502s and high tail latency on long-context invoices generation. We demoed Request Inspector, Request Playback, trace correlation across frontend->proxy->redwood, KV/prefix cache effects, and suggested next steps for a pilot capture.

Topics Covered:
- Where to find request logs and trace IDs in the Console
- Using Request Playback to reproduce failures
- How prefix / KV cache impacts latency and errors
- Debugging model fallbacks and canary rollouts
- Security/operation notes (VPC, KMS, audit logs)

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. I'm Avery Chen from Redwood, I'll run through the playback and the trace view, and Marcus will pull up the live console.
[00:22] Marcus: Cool, I can share my screen — let me know if audio is okay. Samira is here for product context.
[00:31] Priya: Audio is good. We've got a few failing requests that show 502s in our app logs, but it's not clear if it's on your side or our proxy.
[00:45] Marcus: Right, good callout. The first thing is request correlation: you should see a trace id on the API response header, and that same id is searchable in the Console -> Request Inspector.
[01:03] Tom: We tried searching by transaction id, sometimes the trace id looks like 0x2f4a... but the console search returned nothing.
[01:15] Marcus: Two things could be happening — one, the request was routed to a different region/pool; two, prefix cache could be short-circuiting and not creating full traces for cached prefixes. We'll show both.
[01:30] Avery: I'm pulling up the Request Inspector now. You can filter by model, route, and tags. See the timeline bar — each vertical stripe is a stage: ingress, routing, model, egress.
[01:47] Luis: Oh nice, I can see a big spike at the model stage for a few requests. That aligns with the timeouts we saw.
[02:05] Marcus: If you click an individual request you get the token-level timing, and the headers — we also surface the backend error code. Here's a sample that returned 502 with "model-prompt-timeout" in the message.
[02:25] Priya: The 502 says "model overloaded" — but we have reserved capacity right now, so that surprised us.
[02:37] Marcus: Can you check if the request used a pinned variant? We saw some customers accidentally route to a cheaper variant when they hit an autoscaling boundary.
[02:50] Tom: Our routing policy is supposed to be pinned to the v3-large model — I can share the route config after.
[03:05] Marcus: Great. Next, Request Playback — this is the key for reproducing intermittent failures. We can replay an exact request and toggle KV-cache and batching.
[03:18] Avery: I'll start a playback, reusing the original trace id. Playback gives you the same headers, same input, and you can step through the timeline.
[03:35] Speaker 1: (murmur) how about the prefix cache side effects...
[03:42] Marcus: Yep, prefix cache will short-circuit and return faster but sometimes returns a stale cached KV leading to malformed contexts — that can manifest as model errors or hallucinations.
[03:58] Luis: When you say "KV cache off" in playback, does that hit the model every time?
[04:05] Marcus: Exactly — with KV-cache disabled the playback will exercise the full path to the model, so you can see if the model itself errors or if the cache layer caused the bad state.
[04:18] Priya: Cool, can you show one where we toggle KV-cache?
[04:24] Marcus: On it — running playback now. (screen click noises) Ok, playback completed — this run with KV-cache enabled returned a 200 but later we saw content truncation. Now re-run with KV-cache disabled...
[04:44] Marcus: Replayed with KV-cache disabled — this one returned a 502 at the model stage, and you can see the stack trace-ish message: "out-of-memory during quantized kernel" — sometimes transcription shows q-kernel as q-nel but it's the kernel.
[05:05] Tom: Hmm, OOM — we thought dedicated pool had margin. Are there device-level metrics here?
[05:14] Marcus: We surface GPU utilization and per-shard memory pressure in the Console's Metrics tab for Dedicated. If you're hosted, we show aggregate pressure and whether the kernel fallback path was chosen.
[05:29] Avery: Also worth mentioning automatic fallback — if the primary kernel fails we try a slower, memory-friendly kernel. That avoids hard errors but can spike latency; sometimes the fallback itself returns a 502 under pressure.
[05:44] Priya: That matches what we saw — occasional high tails rather than consistent failures.
[05:52] Marcus: Next trick: use the Request Timeline to inspect batching and queue time. We had a customer who misinterpreted average latency — their p95 was fine but p99 was huge because of batching peaks.
[06:08] Luis: Is there a way to see batch sizes over time?
[06:11] Marcus: Yep, under Request Inspector you can toggle the batch histogram which shows batch size distribution and mean queue time.
[06:22] Avery: I'll show a quick example where a long input (3k tokens) caused the batcher to wait for the token threshold — that pushed a subset of requests into a later micro-batch and increased tail latency.
[06:39] Tom: We do have variable lengths — invoice summaries range 200 to 3500 tokens. Any recommendations?
[06:48] Marcus: Two levers: suggest using a request pre-split or token prefiltering to cap tokens for latency sensitive routes, and enable adaptive batching where small short requests are prioritized. We can provide a config recipe.
[07:04] Priya: Can adaptive batching be turned on per-route?
[07:07] Samira: Yes, per-route policies. We'll send the recipe with recommended thresholds for your workload.
[07:15] Marcus: Now security notes: request logs include redacted user content by default; full payload retention is configurable for pilot environments. For VPC/private deployments we support KMS and HSM integrations, audit logs, and SOC 2 controls.
[07:35] Tom: We need audit logs for 90 days and KMS integration — is that supported in hosted pilot?
[07:41] Avery: Hosted can do customer-managed keys via a KMS bridge for dedicated/private; for hosted we can discuss an isolated tenant with restricted retention. We'll follow up in the ticket.
[07:55] Luis: Back to reproducing — when you did playback earlier, what changed in the kernel selection?
[08:01] Marcus: The console flags kernel selection in the trace details — you'll see a "kernel_chosen" field, sometimes it says "quant-opt-v2" and fallback says "quant-safe-v1".
[08:13] Priya: There were a couple of logs where the kernel name was garbled in our exported CSVs — maybe transcription/parsing issue.
[08:21] Marcus: That can happen if we CSV-escape metadata incorrectly; we'll ensure the export is tested for your platform.
[08:33] Speaker 2: (brief cross-talk)
[08:37] Marcus: Quick demo of a trace correlation: front-end logs show request start at 14:02:11, the trace id 0x2f4a... you can map that to the Request Inspector timeline and then expand to see shard-level timings.
[08:54] Tom: I pasted three trace ids in the chat — can you confirm you found them?
[08:58] Marcus: Yep, grabbed them. I'm going to run a targeted playback with the most recent one.
[09:07] Marcus: Playback ran — returned a 200 this time. Differences were tiny tokenization variance and cache hit. You can see the cache hit flagged in the trace meta: "cache: prefix-hit".
[09:22] Priya: So intermittent means sometimes the cache returns stale or malformed state and sometimes it hits model path.
[09:29] Marcus: Correct. Two suggested mitigations: 1) increase prefix cache TTL, 2) instrument a cache validator in the app which fails fast if context checksum mismatch.
[09:44] Luis: Are there built-in validators?
[09:47] Marcus: Not yet as a turnkey, but you can use taggable checks and Redwood logging to synthesize a checksum pipeline; we'll share a snippet.
[09:58] Avery: Another helpful Console feature is the "Request Alerts" — you can set an alert for p99 latency or for any 5xx spike and attach a playbook.
[10:09] Tom: Playbook as in auto-run of playback?
[10:12] Samira: Not auto-run, but a one-click prepopulated playback link + recommended checklist for investigating. We plan to add automated capture in future.
[10:23] Priya: On the auto-capture roadmap — can you share if that will be in hosted or only dedicated?
[10:28] Marcus: The initial rollout will be hosted as a beta, with private/dedicated following.
[10:34] Tom: Any known issues with older quantized models? We saw more failures on the 8bit quant variant.
[10:41] Marcus: Older quant versions can have kernel memory edge cases. We usually recommend trying the newer quant-opt builds; the Console's model catalog shows recommended quant profile per workload.
[10:53] Luis: Is that catalog accessible via API? We want to automate model recommendations in our CI.
[10:58] Avery: Yes, the model catalog is accessible via the Redwood API — we'll include the doc link.
[11:05] Marcus: Quick aside — sometimes seen customers route to Anthropic or OpenAI as fallback; that adds network roundtrip and different error shapes. Worth calling out if you have multi-provider routing.
[11:19] Tom: We're not using fallbacks yet but might consider as resilience. Would that complicate tracing?
[11:25] Marcus: It complicates horizontal correlation but we add provider and puppet metadata in the trace so you can see which provider handled the request.
[11:35] Priya: Ok, let's talk concrete reproduction plan. Marcus, what would you need from us to run a repeatable test?
[11:42] Marcus: Three things: 1) sample request payloads (we asked for Postman collection), 2) trace ids & approximate timestamps, 3) a short SLA matrix detailing desired p50/p95/p99 targets and acceptable fallback behavior.
[11:59] Tom: We'll share those by Tuesday.
[12:03] Priya: Also interested in the console's log export format — can it stream to our ELK?
[12:09] Marcus: Yes, we support pushing audit logs and request traces to customer sinks (S3, CloudWatch, or your ELK) via a connector. We'll share the connector docs.
[12:21] Luis: During playback, I noticed the role attribution was off in a couple of requests — like user ids were missing. Is that redaction?
[12:29] Marcus: By default we redact PII; in pilot we can enable more verbose retention with filters so you get user ids for debugging under strict access controls.
[12:43] Avery: We're also going to run a quick stress test in a sandbox if you want — replaying 500 lamp requests to observe tail behavior.
[12:52] Tom: That'd be helpful. Run it on a dedicated sandbox not prod.
[12:59] Marcus: Agreed. We'll use your sample payloads and run at modest concurrency to avoid disturbing production quotas.
[13:09] Priya: One more — what's the recommended approach for long trace retention? Our compliance asks for 180 days.
[13:18] Avery: We support configurable retention; for hosted there are limits, but for Private/Dedicated we can meet 180 days with appropriate storage add-on. We'll include a cost estimate.
[13:29] Tom: Great.
[13:33] Marcus: Wrapping up, small demo of error analysis in Console: open a failing trace, expand the model node, there's a list of last 20 kernel logs; you can download them as a gzipped tarball for offline forensic.
[13:47] Luis: Handy.
[13:52] Marcus: I'm flagging two likely root causes: kernel memory pressure on large inputs, and an intermittent prefix-cache state corruption. Next steps are deterministic playback, disabling cache to confirm, and stress test.
[14:08] Priya: Anything else on rollout options?
[14:11] Avery: If pilot looks good, we can propose a dedicated pool with reserved headroom and a canary rollout over a week. That gives you isolation and predictable performance.
[14:23] Tom: Sounds reasonable. What's the cost delta roughly?
[14:26] Avery: I'll include a ballpark in the follow-up — depends on shard size and quant profile, we'll model it for your token distribution.
[14:36] Samira: We'll also send the per-route adaptive batching recipe and prefix-cache TTL suggestions.
[14:43] Speaker 3: (laugh) alright thanks all
[14:47] Avery: Okay let's recap quickly.
[14:50] Avery: Action items: Redwood sends playback replay + filter recipe, security & KMS doc, and cost estimate for a dedicated pilot. ZenLedger to provide Postman collection, failing trace IDs, and confirm desired SLOs. Marcus will run a sandbox stress playback and report back.
[15:12] Tom: We can commit to sending the artifacts by Tuesday.
[15:16] Priya: Thanks, this was super actionable.
[15:20] Marcus: Cool — we'll target the follow-ups by Monday/Tuesday next week.
[15:28] Avery: Thanks everyone, we'll close out notes and ship the links.
[47:55] End call.
file_notes: Realistic Fireflies-style transcript with minor transcription artifacts; timestamps approximate to 30-90s cadence. The content focuses on console tracing, request playback, KV/prefix cache, kernel fallbacks, dedicated vs hosted considerations, and next steps for pilot.
